title: How to Protect Your Tax Refund From Identity Theft
excerpt: Learn how to reduce tax refund fraud risk, use an IRS Identity Protection PIN, spot tax scams, and respond if a return is filed in your name.
targetKeyword: how to protect tax refund from identity theft
relatedKeywords: what to do if someone filed taxes in your name
content:
Tax refund identity theft happens when someone uses your Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number to file a tax return and claim a refund before you do. You may not learn about it until your legitimate return is rejected as a duplicate. That is frustrating, but there are practical steps that can lower the risk and help you recover if it happens.

To **protect your tax refund from identity theft**, keep your tax information private, file through a trusted method, secure your IRS account, and consider requesting an IRS Identity Protection PIN. The goal is to make it harder for someone else to file in your name and easier for you to act quickly if there is a problem.

## Know the warning signs

Tax identity theft can appear in several ways. The most common sign is an electronic filing rejection that says a return using your Social Security number has already been submitted. You may also receive an IRS notice about a return you did not file, wages from an employer you do not recognize, or an account you did not open.

Treat those notices seriously, but verify them independently. Do not call a number or click a link from an unexpected email or text. Instead, type IRS.gov into your browser or use the phone number on a notice you have confirmed is legitimate. The IRS does not initiate contact by email, text message, or social media to ask for personal or financial information.

## Protect the information on your tax documents

Your tax return contains information that criminals can use to impersonate you. W-2s, 1099s, prior-year returns, pay stubs, and account statements may include your full name, address, date of birth, and Social Security number. Handle those documents like you would a bank card or passport.

Use these habits throughout the year:

- Store paper tax records in a locked place.
- Shred documents with sensitive information before throwing them away.
- Avoid sending tax documents through unencrypted email or ordinary text messages.
- Use a secure portal when a tax professional offers one.
- Keep your phone, computer, and cloud storage protected with unique passwords and multi-factor authentication.
- Review your credit reports and financial accounts for unfamiliar activity.

Be especially careful around tax season. Scammers often pose as tax software companies, tax preparers, the IRS, or a payroll department. A message that creates urgency, asks for a code, or requests a payment by gift card, crypto, or wire transfer is a strong warning sign.

## File through a trusted method

Filing early can reduce the time in which a criminal could submit a fraudulent return first, but it is not a substitute for account security. File when you have the documents you need and can review the return carefully. Do not rush into using a website or preparer you have not checked.

If you file electronically, use the official website of established tax software or a qualified tax professional. Confirm the web address before entering personal information. Look for a secure connection, but remember that a padlock icon alone does not prove a site is legitimate. Criminals can create convincing copies of real websites.

If you work with a preparer, ask how the firm protects documents, who can access your data, and how it will contact you about questions. The IRS maintains information about choosing a tax return preparer, including credentials and warning signs of questionable practices.

## Consider an IRS Identity Protection PIN

An Identity Protection PIN, often called an IP PIN, is a six-digit number issued by the IRS. It helps the IRS verify that the person filing a federal return is really you. According to the [IRS IP PIN guidance](https://www.irs.gov/identity-theft-fraud-scams/get-an-identity-protection-pin), taxpayers can request one proactively, even if they have not previously experienced tax-related identity theft.

The PIN is different from the five-digit PIN you might use to sign an electronic return. An IP PIN is known only to you and the IRS, and you enter it when prompted by your tax software or preparer. The IRS issues a new IP PIN each calendar year.

Before enrolling, make sure you are on an official IRS page. Never share your IP PIN with anyone except a tax preparer you have chosen and who needs it to prepare your return. The IRS will not call, text, or email asking you to reveal it.

### A few practical IP PIN reminders

- Request it directly through the IRS, not through a link in an unexpected message.
- Keep it in a secure place, not in an unprotected notes app or email draft.
- Tell your preparer only through a secure, verified channel.
- Use the current year's IP PIN when filing, including when filing a prior-year return during the current calendar year.
- Consider whether eligible dependents also need protection, particularly if their Social Security numbers have been exposed.

An IP PIN is a useful layer of protection, but it does not replace safe handling of documents or strong account security.

## Secure your IRS online account and email

Your email account is often the recovery path for tax software, financial institutions, and government accounts. If someone gains access to it, they may be able to intercept password resets or tax notices.

Start with a long, unique password for your email account and turn on multi-factor authentication. Then review recovery email addresses, phone numbers, signed-in devices, forwarding rules, and connected apps. Remove anything you do not recognize.

Apply the same approach to your IRS online account and tax software account. Use a different password for each service. A password manager can create and store strong unique passwords, which is safer than reusing variations of one password.

## Spot tax-season phishing and impostor scams

Tax scammers rely on fear and urgency. They may say your refund is frozen, that you owe tax immediately, or that a payment is waiting if you verify your identity. Their real goal is usually your login, Social Security number, bank account information, or a one-time security code.

Pause before responding to any unexpected tax-related message. A few rules can protect you:

- Do not click links in an unsolicited IRS, tax software, or payroll message.
- Do not read a one-time code to a caller.
- Do not pay a supposed tax debt with gift cards, crypto, or a wire transfer.
- Do not share a photo of your driver's license or tax documents unless you initiated a verified identity-check process.
- Go directly to IRS.gov or the official tax software website to check an account or return status.

For examples of common tax scams and reporting options, see the [IRS identity theft and scams hub](https://www.irs.gov/identity-theft-central).

## What to do if someone filed a tax return in your name

If your return is rejected because one has already been filed, do not keep resubmitting the same electronic return. Save the rejection message and contact the IRS through its official identity theft resources. You may need to file a paper return and submit Form 14039, Identity Theft Affidavit, depending on the circumstances and IRS instructions.

You should also report the identity theft at [IdentityTheft.gov](https://www.identitytheft.gov/). The Federal Trade Commission can provide a personalized recovery plan and documentation to help you deal with affected accounts. Its [tax identity theft guidance](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-tax-identity-theft) explains common signs and next steps.

Keep a simple record as you work: dates, names of representatives, case numbers, copies of notices, and any forms you submit. If you believe a data breach exposed your Social Security number, consider placing a credit freeze with the nationwide credit bureaus. A freeze can help stop someone from opening new credit in your name, though it does not directly prevent a fraudulent tax filing.

## Protect your refund delivery details

Once your return is filed, monitor the bank account or prepaid card where you expect the refund. Use an account you control and review the routing and account numbers before submitting your return. Do not let a preparer direct your refund to an unfamiliar account.

If you receive a refund you were not expecting, do not spend it. Contact the IRS for instructions. An unexpected refund can be a sign that someone used your information to file a false return or redirect money.

## A simple tax-security checklist

### Before filing

- Gather documents from verified sources.
- Secure email and tax software accounts with unique passwords and multi-factor authentication.
- Decide whether to request an IRS IP PIN.
- Choose a trusted filing method or qualified preparer.
- Watch for phishing messages that mention your refund or tax account.

### When filing

- Check the web address before signing in.
- Review your name, address, bank details, and dependents carefully.
- Use your current IP PIN if you have one.
- Save a secure copy of the confirmation and return.

### After filing

- Monitor your refund status only through official channels.
- Keep an eye on mail and IRS notices.
- Securely store the return and supporting documents.
- Act promptly if you receive a duplicate-filing rejection or notice about unfamiliar income.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does filing early stop tax refund identity theft?

Filing once you have accurate documents can reduce the opportunity for a criminal to file first, but it does not guarantee protection. Strong account security, careful document handling, and an IP PIN offer additional protection.

### Is an IRS IP PIN required?

No. Many taxpayers choose one voluntarily as a proactive security measure. The IRS may also assign one in certain identity theft cases. If you have an IP PIN, include it when filing your federal return.

### Can a credit freeze protect my tax refund?

A credit freeze helps prevent new credit accounts from being opened in your name. It does not stop someone from filing a false tax return, so it should be one part of a broader identity-protection plan.

### What should I do if I get a tax-related text message?

Do not click links, reply with personal information, or share a security code. Visit IRS.gov directly if you need to check your account or refund. You can also report suspicious messages through the IRS scam-reporting guidance.

## The bottom line

Tax refund identity theft is easier to manage when you prepare before filing season. Protect tax documents, use secure accounts, file through a verified service, and consider an IRS Identity Protection PIN. If a fraudulent return is filed in your name, keep records and use official IRS and FTC resources right away. A calm, organized response helps protect both your refund and your financial identity.
